rv.q: Reid, Strong and Manville are transfixing as awful revelation after revelation comes to light.
This is a thriller, not a philosophy seminar, quick to switch out currency for timelessness.
Nevertheless, it’s a Grand Guignol finish to what has previously been an effective, affecting and strictly naturalistic new interpretation of this canonical drama.
Aristotle called “Oedipus the King” the perfect tragedy and that still applies in my book, 2,500-odd years later.
Icke's Oedipus is continuously engaging and smart, and it is exceedingly well performed by a cast
It’s election night in Robert Icke’s “Oedipus,” a modern retelling of Sophocles’ “Oedipus the King” that must be the buzziest, if not the chicest, Broadway offering of the fall season.
Those last awful moments of anagnorisis, as Manville and Strong expertly time their performances to the diminishing seconds, are legitimately stomach-turning.

The taut spin on “Oedipus” now on Broadway after a West End run last fall is a rare and magnificent feat of adaptation: Writer and director Robert Icke draws Sophocles’ ancient play into the present while deepening its timeless explorations of power, desire and fate.
Icke's adaptation is an absolute model of Hitchcockian suspense, and the performances could not be better.
We rarely get theatrical tragedy of this scale and intensity, and the modern political world, with its carefully curated imagery and brutal power games, is the perfect setting for it.
Now he has attempted the same feat with Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, often named the world’s greatest play, and the results are thrilling.

Anchored by Mark Strong and Lesley Manville’s riveting performances and driven by Icke’s razor-edged vision, this Oedipus becomes less a revival than a stark reminder that the past—once unearthed—can still detonate the present.
Manville towers above the stage in an unforgettable turn.
And when a play has endured for nearly 2,500 years, it can withstand an extreme home makeover.

Sure, ignorance may indeed be bliss, the truth doesn't always set you free, and, yes, love may be blind. But ending "Oedipus" on an upbeat flashback is the greatest tragedy of this otherwise impressive update.
It's sharply acted and conceptually ambitious.
But Mark Strong and Lesley Manville's turns as Oedipus and Jocasta give this take on the Greek classic a grounded yet otherworldly sense of magnificent devastation.
His Oedipus, while glowing with his usual whip-smart language, doesn't have much fun in the toppling.

Icke makes two promises of his own to the audience, in a production now on Broadway that stands out for its exceptional cast, with performances of remarkable intensity by Mark Strong as Oedipus and especially Lesley Manville as Jocasta, making a much-welcomed Broadway debut.
Ickes’s freehanded adaptation of this classic cautionary tale, though superficially timely, does little to address the miscarriages of justice we’re forced to witness daily.
In the end, Ickes’ updating turns the Sophocles classic into a parody.
Ickes and his cast have achieved something truly remarkable, producing a classic that doesn't feel like a revival at all.

Icke’s adaptation, Oedipus—now playing at Studio 54 on Broadway—grips the audience by the throat from the outset, slowly tightening its grip as the minutes tick by (literally, with an onstage countdown clock) leading to its devastating conclusion.
It’s an astonishing piece of work, one that has only deepened and darkened on its journey across the Atlantic.
Robert Icke’s modern Oedipus proves that even when we know the ending, watching the civic body destroy itself in real-time remains devastatingly compelling.
Oedipus is striking in its relevance and entrancing in its performance.

cn.t: Robert Icke's sleek political thriller adaptation earns strong praise for Mark Strong and Lesley Manville's performances and timely resonance, though some critics find the extended pacing dilutes Sophocles' original urgency.

sg.vl: Center Orchestra front-to-mid is the house sweet spot
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both identify center Orchestra Rows A-E as offering the most direct, immersive sightlines. The stage's setback (per TickPick) enhances Row A viewing, and Rows F-H avoid the Front Mezzanine overhang that begins at Row M. Headout lists 15 orchestra rows (A-P) totaling ~521-538 seats depending on source.

SeatPlan explicitly flags Rows F-H as 'good value seats' that avoid Front Mezzanine overhang disruption and sit at a comfortable distance from the stage. Headout and TickPick echo the value framing for this band. Pricing typically below the Row A-E premium band.

SeatPlan describes Center Front Mezz AA-BB as 'very popular' with 'excellently raked seats and expansive overhead sightlines.' No Rear Mezz overhang exists above this section. Headout prices most Center Front Mezz seats around $224. Row AA safety rail can clip the stage for shorter patrons, so Row BB is the refined pick.

SeatPlan: Left-section Front Mezz has 'more restricted sightlines of action at the corner of stage right'; Right section mirrors this toward stage left. Legroom described as 'particularly cramped' at side seats. Still elevated with no overhang above, so sightlines to center stage remain workable.

SeatPlan calls 'rows FF and GG in the Center Rear Mezzanine' the Rear Mezz sweet spot; Headout flags EE-GG as good value ('a good look at the stage without costing as much'). Row EE sits directly behind a horizontal aisle per the SeatPlan overview. Steep rake trades legroom for sightlines.

sg.vl: Side-angle obstruction into opposite stage half
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both warn that Left Rear Mezz Rows HH-NN have obstructed sightlines into stage right, and Right Rear Mezz mirrors this to stage left. Combined with the steep rake, tight legroom, and distance, these rows deliver the weakest experience in the house.
